title: A Systematic Comparison of Multilingual Interpretability MethodsReveals Anisotropy-Driven Failures

paper.title: A Systematic Comparison of Multilingual Interpretability Methods Reveals Anisotropy-Driven Failures
paper.abstract:
Abstract Multilingual language models develop shared cross-lingual representations, and various interpretability methods claim to quantify this sharing.
These methods have been developed largely in isolation, and when they disagree, it is unclear whether the disagreement reflects a property of the model or an artifact of the measurement.
We compare four sharing metrics —CKA, ANC, GMM dominance per token, and ILO —across 21 base models from five families (125M–14B parameters) and correlate each with cross-lingual transfer on five downstream tasks.
We find that the metrics differ in their quantification of cross-lingual sharing in these models and suggest that the disagreement traces to anisotropy , the tendency of representations to cluster in a narrow cone of the embedding space.
Only ILO’s correlation with cross-lingual transfer (Spearman’s ρ = 0.90 \rho=0.90 ) survives controls for model size, family, and per-task variation.
We therefore recommend ILO as the primary sharing metric, to be reported alongside anisotropy diagnostics.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Multilingual language models develop shared representations across languages without explicit alignment supervision ( Pires et al., 2019 ; Wu and Dredze, 2019 ) . A growing set of interpretability methods now claims to measure this sharing: probing classifiers, similarity metrics, distributional approaches, and neuron-level analyses. These methods have largely been developed in isolation, on one or two model families at a time. When different metrics on different models yield different conclusions, it is unclear whether the disagreement reflects genuine differences between models or is an artifact of the measurement itself. This ambiguity is especially concerning as contextual embeddings often exhibit anisotropy : they occupy a narrow cone in the representation space, rather than spreading evenly in all directions ( isotropy ), with variance concentrated in a few dimensions ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ; Timkey and van Schijndel, 2021 ) , as shown in Figure 1 . Anisotropy poses at least two risks for any geometric measure of cross-lingual sharing: First, it inflates apparent similarity, making any two vectors look close by default. Second, it confines meaningful variation to a low-dimensional subspace, so any metric sensitive to dominant directions of variance —whether it explicitly projects onto them or implicitly up-weights them —will be driven by that subspace rather than by the full representational geometry. Because conclusions about which architectures, training regimes, and scaling choices yield stronger cross-lingual sharing are only as reliable as the metrics on which they rest, it matters whether metrics can be trusted to track sharing through anisotropy. This paper therefore examines how this distortion affects the metrics under consideration, and assesses which, if any, can be relied on to reflect genuine cross-lingual sharing. Concretely, we address three questions through a systematic comparison of four sharing metrics across 21 base models from five families (BLOOM, OPT, XGLM, Qwen3, SmolLM3; 125M–14B parameters), supplemented by instruction-tuned variants and intermediate checkpoints: • How do multilingual models share representations across languages? • When do existing metrics agree or disagree as to the degree of cross-lingual sharing? • Which metric best predicts cross-lingual transfer? Our answers, anticipating § 4 : models exhibit three sharing patterns rather than a binary split implied by metrics dominated by high-variance directions, and the metric disagreement traces directly to anisotropy, with language probes showing that language identity is relocated to the directions such metrics discard or down-weight. Among the four metrics, ILO ( Wilie et al., 2025 ) is the only one whose association with cross-lingual transfer survives controls for size, family, and per-task variation, reaching a Spearman rank correlation of ρ = 0.90 \rho=0.90 ; ANC ( Del and Fishel, 2022 ) forms a clear second tier whose association rests on between-family contrasts, while PCA-based GMM dominance per token ( Shani and Basirat, 2025 ) has a within-family signal too weak to characterize as a relationship across matched architectures and CKA ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) shows no association at any level. We therefore recommend ILO as the primary sharing metric, and further suggest that it should be reported alongside anisotropy diagnostics.

sections.heading: Measuring cross-lingual sharing
sections.text: Multilingual models develop shared representations between languages without explicit alignment supervision ( Pires et al., 2019 ; Wu and Dredze, 2019 ) . The contributing factors remain debated; shared positional embeddings, similar word order, parameter sharing across languages, and training-data imbalance have all been proposed as drivers ( Dufter and Schütze, 2020 ; Conneau et al., 2020b ; Schäfer et al., 2024 ) . A series of measures has been developed to quantify cross-lingual sharing: Similarity-based metrics compare activation patterns across languages on parallel input. Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA; Kornblith et al., 2019 ) measures global geometric similarity between cross-lingual representation matrices. Average Neuron Correlation (ANC; Del and Fishel, 2022 ) captures per-neuron alignment. Lens-based methods such as the logit lens ( nostalgebraist, 2020 ) project intermediate hidden states into the vocabulary. Wendler et al. (2024) use this to argue that Llama-2 routes multilingual inputs through English-aligned representations. Subsequent work has questioned both the technique ( Belrose et al., 2025 ) and the claim itself: apparent reliance on English varies with training data balance, and representations often mix from several languages rather than being pivoted toward English ( Zhong et al., 2025 ; Schut et al., 2025 ; Trinley et al., 2025 ; Harrasse et al., 2026 ) . Shani and Basirat (2025) present a mixture model-based metric : they fit Gaussian mixture models over PCA-projected representations and use them to derive language dominance scores. Wilie et al. (2025) introduce Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO), a neighborhood-based metric that operates on the full hidden state. Finally, neuron-level analyses identify units that activate selectively per language, using activation entropy ( Tang et al., 2024 ; Kojima et al., 2024 ) , ternary classifications ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , sparse autoencoders ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , or transcoders ( Harrasse et al., 2026 ) . A parallel line of work scores each language by its directed alignment with English and validates it against downstream performance, at the language level in MEXA ( Kargaran et al., 2025 ) and at the instance level in DALI ( Ravisankar et al., 2026 ) . These primarily measure alignment with English rather than sharing among all languages, which is what the four metrics we compare quantify; we relate the two views in Appendix C.4 . All of these methods have largely been developed and evaluated in isolation. Comparisons typically restrict themselves to one or two model families, leaving open whether disagreements between metrics reflect substantive differences between models or measurement artifacts. Filling this gap, we compare four representative metrics —spanning similarity-based, distributional, and neighborhood approaches —on the same set of models (§ 4 ).

sections.heading: Representational anisotropy
sections.text: Contextual embeddings from transformer models tend to occupy a narrow cone in representation space rather than filling it isotropically, with most pairs of vectors having high cosine similarity regardless of their semantic content ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ; Gao et al., 2019 ) . Biś et al. (2021) argue that much of this apparent anisotropy stems from a common shift shared across embeddings: once the mean is subtracted, the residual distribution is closer to isotropic. Other proposed causes of anisotropy include self-attention dynamics ( Godey et al., 2024 ) and optimizer-level effects in Adam ( Stollenwerk and Stollenwerk, 2025 ) . Regardless of cause, anisotropy distorts geometric analyses of representations. Rajaee and Pilehvar (2022) and Hämmerl et al. (2023) document anisotropy in multilingual models specifically, and show that post-hoc isotropy enhancement improves cross-lingual semantic similarity —indicating that anisotropy can mask genuine cross-lingual structure. How isotropy should be measured is itself contested ( Rudman et al., 2022 ) , and anisotropy is not uniformly harmful: it has limited impact on sentence-representation expressiveness for clustering ( Ait-Saada and Nadif, 2023 ) , is incompatible with cluster structure by construction ( Mickus et al., 2024 ) , and decreasing isotropy during finetuning can improve downstream performance ( Rudman and Eickhoff, 2024 ) . Our concern is not whether anisotropy is desirable in a model, but what it does to the metrics used to measure cross-lingual sharing (§ 4.2 ); our own diagnosis there rests on effective dimensionality and probing rather than on the cosine diagnostic alone.

sections.heading: 3 Experimental Setup
sections.text: In our main experiments, we compute four cross-lingual sharing metrics across 21 models. This section presents these metrics and models along with the data we used and our statistical framework.

sections.heading: 3.1 Sharing Metrics
sections.text: We select one metric from each of the main methodological families of representation-level cross-lingual analysis, so that the comparison contrasts kinds of measurement rather than variants of one kind: CKA for global geometric similarity, ANC for neuron-level correspondence, λ \lambda for distributional structure, and ILO for local neighborhood overlap. The metrics are: • (Linear) CKA (Centered Kernel Alignment; Kornblith et al., 2019 ) is the established geometric-similarity baseline. It measures the similarity between two representation spaces by comparing their pairwise distance structures —specifically, how consistently pairs of representations that are similar in one space are also similar in the other. Values range from 0 (no shared structure) to 1 (identical up to isotropic scaling and orthogonal transformation). • ANC (Average Neuron-Wise Correlation; Del and Fishel, 2022 ) measures whether individual neurons carry consistent activation patterns across languages —in contrast to CKA, which measures whether the overall pairwise similarity structure is preserved across representations. For each neuron, ANC computes the absolute Pearson correlation between its activations on parallel sentences in two languages. Averaging over neurons yields a value in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , where 1 indicates that every neuron responds identically (up to sign differences) across languages. • GMM dominance per token. Shani and Basirat (2025) fit a supervised Gaussian Mixture Model in a PCA subspace retaining 98% of variance and report the fraction of tokens whose likelihood is higher in a foreign-language space than in their own. We refer to this quantity as λ \lambda and report it by layer after subsampling each language to 10,000 tokens before PCA and GMM fitting. This matches the subsampling used for ILO and removes tokenizer-fertility bias as a confound when comparing across families with different scripts. Unbalanced word-level and sentence-level variants appear in Appendix A.2 . • ILO (Interlingual Local Overlap; Wilie et al., 2025 ) quantifies cross-lingual sharing via k k -nearest-neighbor queries ( k = 5 k=5 ) in the full representation space, combining bridge scores (how often a token’s neighbors include other languages) and reachability scores (the fraction of other languages that appear in the k k -nearest-neighbor set of any token of that language) into a single index ranging from 0 (complete separation) to 1 (complete sharing). We compute ILO on token-level representations with the same 10,000-tokens-per-language subsample as λ \lambda , which controls tokenizer fertility. The released implementation of Wilie et al. (2025) instead operates on mean-pooled sentence embeddings; we report that variant in Appendix B.5 . We additionally report a centered variant (ILO c ), computed identically after subtracting the per-layer mean hidden state across all tokens and languages, which removes anisotropy-driven neighborhood structure that can inflate apparent sharing.

sections.heading: 3.2 Models
sections.text: Our 21 base models come from five model families, spanning 125M to 14B parameters and varying in training data composition and scale. We briefly introduce the model families here; see Appendix A.1 for full details on models and checkpoints. • BLOOM BigScience Workshop et al. (2023) (560M–7.1B) is trained on 350B tokens of the ROOTS corpus Laurençon et al. (2022) . It covers 46 natural languages with ca. 70% non-English data, and provides pretraining checkpoints. • XGLM Lin et al. (2022) (564M–7.5B) is trained on 30 languages drawn from CC100-XL. We use both BLOOM and XGLM despite their age because the sharing metrics we evaluate were validated on these families: Shani and Basirat (2025) report λ \lambda on BLOOM and Del and Fishel (2022) report ANC on XGLM. • OPT Zhang et al. (2022) (125M–6.7B) serves as our non-multilingual baseline. It is trained on 180B predominantly English tokens from the Pile Gao et al. (2020) , BookCorpus, and CC-News, with only incidental non-English content from Common Crawl. • Qwen3 Yang et al. (2025) (0.6B–14B) provides a modern high-compute comparison. It is trained on ca. 36T tokens spanning 119 languages and dialects, though exact proportions are undisclosed. • SmolLM3 Bakouch et al. (2025) (3B) is trained on 11.2T tokens drawn primarily from FineWeb-Edu, FineWeb-2, and DCLM, with ca. 12% multilingual web data natively supporting six languages (English, French, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese) plus additional training on Arabic, Chinese, and Russian; it uniquely provides intermediate checkpoints across three training stages for studying multilingual representations during pre- and post-training. We additionally characterize instruction-tuned variants —BLOOMZ Muennighoff et al. (2023) , Qwen3 non-Base, SmolLM3-Instruct —and 59 intermediate checkpoints from BLOOM and SmolLM3, yielding a total of 32 model configurations plus checkpoints. Instruction-tuned variants contribute to representational characterization but are excluded from transfer analysis; all transfer correlations are based on the 21 base models. This is because our transfer protocol finetunes on English data and evaluates zero-shot (§ 3.4 ), measuring what the pretraining geometry makes possible; on instruction-tuned variants it would entangle sharing with post-training recipes that differ across families. The question we do ask about post-training—whether it changes the sharing structure—is addressed in § 4.4 .

sections.heading: 3.3 Data
sections.text: All interpretability analyses use the FLORES-200 NLLB Team et al. (2022) devtest set, providing 1,012 parallel sentences across ten languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, German, Japanese, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, and Turkish. These languages span four scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, CJK), multiple typological families (Romance, Germanic, Turkic, Japonic, Sino-Tibetan, Semitic, Slavic), and a range of morphological types (isolating, fusional, agglutinative). Sentence-level pairs are required by CKA and ANC, which compute cross-lingual similarity from aligned representations; the remaining methods operate on monolingual representations.

sections.heading: 3.4 Cross-Lingual Transfer Evaluation
sections.text: We use zero-shot cross-lingual transfer as a functional validation criterion, not as ground truth for sharing: transfer has drivers beyond representational alignment, among them task format, vocabulary overlap, and target-language pretraining exposure, which is why we average over five tasks, require associations to survive a number of controls (§ 3.5 ), and keep the diagnosis of the disagreement between methods (§ 4.2 ) independent of transfer. We fine-tune each of the 21 base models on English training data and evaluate zero-shot on up to nine non-English languages (coverage varies by task; Appendix A.5 ) across five tasks: Belebele (reading comprehension; Bandarkar et al., 2024 ), XNLI (natural language inference; Conneau et al., 2018 ), XCSR (commonsense reasoning; Lin et al., 2021 ), SIB-200 (topic classification; Adelani et al., 2024 ), and XQuAD (extractive question answering; Artetxe et al., 2020 ). As an aggregate per-model metric, we compute, for each task, the mean accuracy over the non-English target languages that task covers, and then take the unweighted mean of these five per-task means. We refer to this number as the transfer score . For each model–task pair, we sweep over 3–5 learning rates between 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} and 10 − 4 10^{-4} , with ranges adapted to the model family’s stable regime. We use AdamW with linear warmup (10% of steps), weight decay 0.01, and gradient clipping at 1.0. Task-specific epoch counts range from 3 to 20. The best learning rate is selected for each model–task pair based on validation accuracy. Full hyperparameters are in Appendix A.6 . Because the § 4.3 correlations link base model metrics to finetuned model behavior, we re-apply the full interpretability suite after finetuning to verify that the base model geometry survives.

sections.heading: 3.5 Statistical Framework
sections.text: Beyond characterizing representations, we test for functional relevance: whether sharing metrics correlate with cross-lingual transfer, and whether any association survives controls for model size, family membership, and task choice.

sections.heading: Primary correlation
sections.text: We use Spearman rank correlations ( ρ \rho ) for all tests. The primary correlation is computed across all models relative to the transfer score defined in § 3.4 .

sections.heading: Decompositions
sections.text: We report three additional analyses to check whether the primary correlation is robust. Per-family ρ \rho separates between- from within-family contributions to the cross-model association. Per-task ρ \rho for each metric against each task (4 metrics × \times 5 tasks = = 20 tests) shows whether the primary correlation holds task by task. Because running 20 tests simultaneously inflates the family-wise false-positive rate, we apply the Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) procedure, which bounds the expected proportion of false discoveries among reported associations at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 . This ensures that a pattern such as a correlation being significant across all five tasks reflects a consistent relationship rather than accumulated chance. Partial Spearman ρ \rho controlling for log 10 \log_{10} parameter size checks that the sharing–transfer association is not reducible to a model-size effect. Within most families, parameter count correlates with both cross-lingual sharing and transfer performance, raising the possibility that any observed association between sharing and transfer is a spurious consequence of larger models doing everything better rather than a genuine relationship between the two. Partialling out log 10 \log_{10} parameters removes the variance in both sharing and transfer that is attributable to size, so that the residual correlation reflects whether sharing predicts transfer over and above what model size alone would explain.

sections.heading: Permutation tests
sections.text: Given our small sample size, we verify significance with non-parametric permutation tests. Each test recomputes ρ \rho on 10,000 random shuffles of the transfer score values to estimate the null distribution, from which we compute a one-tailed p p -value as the proportion of recomputed ρ \rho values greater than or equal to the observed ρ \rho . We run two designs: The first shuffles across all models, testing whether any monotonic association exists. The second shuffles within each family only, testing whether the association persists once between-family contrasts are removed. Family membership is otherwise a confound: model families differ systematically in both architecture and training data, so the cross-model correlation could be driven entirely by between-family contrasts.

sections.heading: 3.6 Additional Diagnostics
sections.text: In addition to the sharing metrics, we report two diagnostics at each layer. Effective dimensionality ( n pca n_{\text{pca}} ) is the number of PCA components needed to retain 98% of variance; small values relative to the full number of dimensions indicate that representations occupy a low-dimensional subspace. Mean random cosine similarity is the average cosine between 5,000 random pairs of hidden states; high values indicate the “narrow cone” geometry where any two vectors look similar by default ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ) , biasing similarity-based measures upward. Together, these metrics flag layers where sharing metrics should be interpreted with caution.

sections.heading: 4 Results and Discussion
sections.text: This section presents our main results together with additional analyses, and discusses our findings. We organize the section around four questions:

sections.heading: 4.1 How Do Models Share Representations Across Languages?
sections.text: When we apply the four metrics across our 21 base models, three distinct sharing patterns emerge (cf. Table 1 , Figure 2 ). • Pattern 1: Concentrated sharing (BLOOM ≥ {\geq} 1B, Qwen3, SmolLM3): high λ \lambda ( > 0.75 >0.75 ), high ILO, and variance concentrated in just n pca = 2 n_{\text{pca}}=2 dimensions at the peak λ \lambda layer. The sharing metrics increase through the middle layers and fall toward the output, producing the inverted-U profile visible in Figure 2 . • Pattern 2: Distributed sharing (XGLM): high ILO ( 0.44 0.44 at 4.5B, comparable to BLOOM-7.1B’s 0.40 0.40 ) but near-zero λ \lambda , with variance distributed across thousands of dimensions ( n pca n_{\text{pca}} in the thousands at every layer). • Pattern 3: Minimal sharing (OPT): low values on every metric, consistent with OPT’s predominantly English training data. The critical case is XGLM. GMM dominance per token used in isolation groups XGLM with OPT, despite XGLM’s transfer score ( 0.55 0.55 ) approaching BLOOM-7.1B ( 0.60 0.60 ) and clearly exceeding OPT-6.7B ( 0.41 0.41 ). The remaining metrics tell a coherent story: across all 21 models, ANC spans 0.34 0.34 – 0.68 0.68 and tracks the sharing patterns, while CKA falls in a narrow band ( 0.58 0.58 – 0.73 0.73 ) and discriminates poorly across families. sections.heading: 4.2 Why Do Methods Disagree?
sections.text: The metric disagreement in § 4.1 is not arbitrary: each metric has a measurable sensitivity to representational anisotropy, and language probes locate where language identity is actually encoded.

sections.heading: Anisotropy sensitivity differs across metrics
sections.text: Mean random cosine similarity ( cos ¯ \overline{\cos} ) at peak-sharing layers ranges from 0.86 0.86 (BLOOM-560M) to 0.99 0.99 (several models), indicating that representations occupy a narrow cone where random vectors are similar by default ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ) . The four metrics differ in how this geometry affects them. CKA measures absolute geometric similarity and is inflated by the shared cone direction, consistent with its narrow cross-family range (Table 1 ). ANC computes per-neuron Pearson correlations between parallel-sentence activations; because Pearson subtracts each neuron’s mean, ANC is invariant to the common-shift component of anisotropy ( Biś et al., 2021 ) , consistent with its stronger cross-family discrimination relative to CKA. ILO’s cosine kNN is invariant to per-vector scaling but sensitive to a shared mean shift. The centered variant ILO c (§ 3.1 ) tests this directly: across all 21 models the mean | Δ | |\Delta| is 0.003 0.003 (Appendix B.4 ), so this shift does not appreciably inflate the reported ILO scores. These results are empirical, not architectural: a model with a stronger or differently-shaped cone could show a larger centering shift, and the metric ranking could change accordingly. The disagreement also does not reduce to the metrics’ different input units: CKA and ANC compare the same mean-pooled sentence embeddings yet correlate with transfer at ρ = 0.14 \rho=0.14 and 0.84 0.84 , and λ \lambda and ILO share the same token-level representations yet give opposite verdicts on XGLM (Appendix B.1 ). A more severe failure mode affects a different class of metrics: those that first reduce dimensionality by variance and then measure structure in whatever survives the reduction. We examine this class next through λ \lambda .

sections.heading: Variance-ranked projection collapses the measurement space
sections.text: The λ \lambda pipeline retains PCA components that cover 98% of the variance before clustering. This splits our 21 models into two clearly separated categories: every high- λ \lambda model has n pca = 2 n_{\text{pca}}=2 at its peak- λ \lambda layer, regardless of whether the full hidden dimensionality is 1,024 1{,}024 or 5,120 5{,}120 , while every low- λ \lambda model retains ≥ 20 \geq 20 components. The split is not an artifact of the threshold; it persists at 90% retention (Appendix B.2 ). High λ \lambda therefore reports cluster structure in a 2-dimensional plane while ignoring the remaining hundreds or thousands of potentially meaningful directions. For models where n pca n_{\text{pca}} is larger (XGLM, OPT), no low-dimensional clustering plane exists for the GMM to fit, and λ \lambda stays near zero by construction.

sections.heading: Language identity is relocated, not destroyed
sections.text: To better understand the collapse, we test whether language identity persists outside the principal components: at each layer we train an L 2 L_{2} -regularized logistic-regression probe on the full hidden state, on the PCA principal subspace (top components covering 98% of variance), and on its orthogonal complement (the residual subspace; setup in Appendix A.4 ). Accuracy in the principal subspace reflects language information in the directions GMM dominance can “see”; accuracy in the residual subspace reflects what it discards. At layers with high λ \lambda , principal-subspace accuracy drops to chance levels, while residual-subspace accuracy reaches 96 96 – 99 % 99\% (Figure 3 ). The pattern holds across BLOOM-7.1B (layers 7–19), Qwen3 (a contiguous band of 19–23 layers, depending on scale), and SmolLM3-3B (layers 1–28). Language identity is not destroyed at sharing layers; it is relocated to the directions that a variance-ranked projection discards. This is problematic since the λ \lambda procedure fits Gaussian components labeled by language and asks how often each token has higher likelihood under a foreign-language component than its own, which requires language identity to be at least partially recoverable in the subspace it operates on. Therefore, high λ \lambda in this regime measures how a language-labeled mixture model behaves in a subspace from which language has already been removed and does not measure cross-lingual sharing in any geometric sense. Probe results for all models are in Appendix B.3 . None of this shows that anisotropy is itself harmful to models: the two families with the strongest transfer, Qwen3 and SmolLM3, are also the most extreme on our anisotropy diagnostics ( n pca = 2 n_{\text{pca}}=2 at their peak-sharing layer, cos ¯ = 0.99 \overline{\cos}=0.99 ; Table 1 ), so anisotropy is bad for certain measurements of sharing, not for transfer itself. The curves correspond to the full space, the principal subspace (top components covering 98% of variance), the residual subspace, and a random baseline at 0.1 0.1 .

sections.heading: 4.3 Do Interpretability Methods Predict Cross-Lingual Transfer?
sections.text: To see whether interpretability metrics predict cross-lingual transfer, we correlate them with the transfer score defined in § 3.4 . Per-task and per-language results are in Appendix B.7 , per-language correlations in Appendix C.4 , and all statistical results are in Appendix C . sections.heading: ILO predicts transfer
sections.text: Figure 4 shows the primary association: peak ILO and transfer score are monotonically related across all models. Each family occupies a distinct range of ILO values, so the cross-model correlation reflects both between- and within-family contributions; we disentangle these in the robustness analyses below. Table 2 summarizes all four metrics. ILO is the strongest predictor ( ρ = 0.90 \rho=0.90 ), ANC forms a second tier ( ρ = 0.84 \rho=0.84 ), λ \lambda shows a moderate cross-model association ( ρ = 0.52 \rho=0.52 ), and CKA is near zero ( ρ = 0.14 \rho=0.14 ).

sections.heading: The association is robust for ILO only
sections.text: We perform three checks to separate metrics that capture a sharing-transfer relationship from those that capture confounds: First, we control for log 10 \log_{10} parameters via partial correlation; this leaves λ \lambda , ILO, and ANC largely unchanged (Table 2 ), so model size does not account for the associations. Second, we perform Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate correction; this is survived by ILO and ANC on all five tasks, by λ \lambda on two of them (Belebele and XQuAD), and by CKA on none. Finally, we do a permutation test that shuffles transfer only within families; this confirms ILO ( p = .014 p=.014 ) but not CKA ( p = 0.93 p=0.93 ), ANC ( p = 0.40 p=0.40 ), or λ \lambda ( p = 0.056 p=0.056 ). Excluding the non-multilingual OPT baseline gives the same picture: ILO remains the strongest predictor ( ρ = 0.78 \rho=0.78 ), while ANC drops ( ρ = 0.64 \rho=0.64 ; per-family and per-task breakdowns in Appendix C.2 ). Thus ILO is the only metric whose association survives all three controls; ANC’s rests on between-family contrasts, and CKA shows none at any level. Note that these results are associational, not causal, as training data, architecture, and scale co-vary across families. However, ILO and zero-shot transfer both depend on the local mixing of languages in representation space, so one could claim that ILO’s stronger correlation partly reflects that it is the metric closest in form to our criterion. But the same can be argued for λ \lambda , which shows the opposite result. We therefore recommend ILO as the metric that withstands our controls and the transfer-independent anisotropy centering check (§ 4.2 ), not as a validated measure of sharing.

sections.heading: Sharing emerges through abrupt phase transitions
sections.text: Using intermediate checkpoints from BLOOM (30 across 5 sizes) and SmolLM3 (29 across 3 stages), λ \lambda and ILO undergo coincident jumps at specific training steps rather than rising gradually. In BLOOM-1b1, both metrics jump in lockstep between steps 10K and 100K ( λ \lambda : 0.13 → 0.79 0.13\to 0.79 ); BLOOM-560M never makes this transition (peak λ = 0.26 \lambda=0.26 ). The capacity threshold for BLOOM sits between 560M and 1.1B, but it is architecture- and not size-specific, since the similarly sized Qwen3-0.6B exhibits strong sharing ( λ = 0.92 \lambda=0.92 ). SmolLM3 establishes sharing at its earliest checkpoint ( λ = 0.81 \lambda=0.81 at step 40K) and then the late Stage 3 reasoning training expands the high- λ \lambda zone from 22 to 30 layers. Per-checkpoint results are in Appendix B.8 .

sections.heading: Instruction tuning can induce sharing
sections.text: Because our metrics describe each model at a single training snapshot, instruction-tuned variants, a second snapshot of the same model, let us test whether the three sharing patterns of § 4.1 are stable model properties and whether post-training itself reshapes sharing. BLOOM-560M, for which our metrics never indicate multilingual sharing, develops a 10-layer collapsed-dimensionality zone after instruction tuning (BLOOMZ-560m), where peak λ \lambda rises from 0.21 0.21 to 0.84 0.84 and peak ILO from 0.25 0.25 to 0.37 0.37 , with n pca = 2 n_{\text{pca}}=2 at the new peak layer. The effect then attenuates at scale, where BLOOMZ-7.1B and Qwen3-8B-Instruct show only modest shifts. Full before/after metric results are in Appendix B.9 . They suggest that sharing is not fixed at the end of pretraining: it can emerge through instruction tuning in small models and reorganize through midtraining in larger ones.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: Cross-lingual sharing metrics have been developed and evaluated largely in isolation, leaving open whether disagreements between them reflect genuine differences between models or artifacts of measurement. Our systematic comparison across 21 base models from five families shows that the latter dominates: representational anisotropy makes GMM dominance per token, reliant on PCA, report sharing where probes show language identity has merely been relocated to discarded dimensions, and miss sharing where it is distributed across thousands of directions. This conflates three distinct sharing patterns—concentrated, distributed, and minimal—by collapsing the latter two into a single near-zero score. Among the four metrics tested, only ILO’s association with cross-lingual transfer survives controls for model size, family membership, and per-task decomposition. The practical implication for interpretability practice is that geometric sharing scores cannot be read independently of the geometry they sit in. We recommend reporting metrics alongside anisotropy diagnostics, such as effective dimensionality and mean random cosine similarity at a minimum, so that a reader can tell whether a high score reflects cross-lingual sharing or anisotropic collapse. These results are corrective rather than dismissive of global sharing metrics: a single global score remains the right instrument for quantifying and comparing sharing across models, while explaining how sharing is implemented calls for mechanistic methods ( Tang et al., 2024 ; Kojima et al., 2024 ; Deng et al., 2025 ; Harrasse et al., 2026 ) , which, insofar as they too read structure off anisotropic geometry, likewise benefit from anisotropy diagnostics. Ultimately, these metrics are instruments for understanding models and guiding the development of new models that improve sharing of representations across languages, a role they can play only when they measure what we mean to track.

sections.heading: Future work
sections.text: Concentrated sharing always coincides with low n pca n_{\text{pca}} at the peak layer, but our observational design cannot tell whether this bottleneck actively forces language-agnostic computation or is incidental. Optimizers that suppress anisotropy, such as Coupled Adam ( Stollenwerk and Stollenwerk, 2025 ) , offer a clean intervention to test both this question and whether our metric reliability ranking holds under different anisotropy profiles. Controlled training with matched architectures and varied data composition would further isolate the factors driving the three sharing patterns. Future work also includes applying purpose-built isotropy measures such as IsoScore ( Rudman et al., 2022 ) and extending the comparison to multilingual encoders.

sections.heading: Small and non-independent sample
sections.text: Our 21 models from five families share architecture, data, and tokenizer within each family, making the effective between-family sample size closer to five. We address this through within-family analyses, partial correlations, and within-family permutation tests (§ 4.3 ), but statistical power remains limited. SmolLM3 is represented by a single model size, and detailed per-language training data proportions are publicly available only for BLOOM, preventing direct analysis of how data composition relates to sharing patterns.

sections.heading: Generalization of metric reliability
sections.text: The reliability ranking we report ( λ \lambda heavily anisotropy-sensitive, CKA weakly discriminative, ILO and ANC more robust) holds across the 21 models in this study. Models with substantially higher anisotropy, or with anisotropy modes we did not encounter, may shift this ranking. The takeaway is therefore not that ILO and ANC are universally safe but that anisotropy diagnostics should be reported alongside any geometric sharing metric.

sections.heading: Decoder-only models
sections.text: All 21 models we study are decoder-only language models, whereas much of the cross-lingual sharing literature was built on multilingual encoders ( Pires et al., 2019 ; Conneau et al., 2020a ) , which differ in training objective and attention pattern and in which anisotropy has been documented independently ( Rajaee and Pilehvar, 2022 ) . Whether the reliability ranking we report transfers to encoders is untested, and we make no claim about them.

sections.heading: Language selection and coverage
sections.text: The ten evaluation languages are those reasonably covered by all five transfer benchmarks and by all five model families, and the restriction is deliberate: admitting languages that only some benchmarks or families support would make each model’s transfer score depend on which languages happened to be available for it, and the cross-model comparison would no longer be like-for-like. Even within this set coverage is not complete (XCSR omits Turkish, XNLI omits Japanese and Portuguese, and XQuAD omits Japanese, French, and Portuguese; Appendix B.7 ), which is one reason we average over the languages a task does cover. Two ramifications follow. First, the ten languages are comparatively high-resource and three are Romance, so per-language patterns may be biased toward Romance, and our conclusions concern sharing among well-represented languages. Second, we cannot say from these data whether ILO remains the most reliable metric, or whether λ \lambda fails in the same way, for languages thinly represented in pretraining, the regime where a practitioner would most want a trustworthy sharing metric; testing this requires benchmarks with wider coverage and is left to future work.

sections.heading: Observational design
sections.text: All reported correlations are associational. Common causes such as training data diversity, which promotes both sharing and transfer simultaneously, remain plausible. Controlled interventions would be needed to isolate causal mechanisms.

sections.heading: Hyperparameter sensitivity and confounds
sections.text: We follow Shani and Basirat (2025) for the 98% PCA variance threshold and Wilie et al. (2025) for ILO parameters ( k = 5 k=5 , τ = 3 \tau=3 ) without systematic sensitivity analysis. ILO is also the most computationally expensive of the four metrics; asymptotic time and memory costs for all four are given in Appendix A.3 . All sharing metrics show some correlation with tokenizer vocabulary overlap ( ρ ≈ 0.33 \rho\approx 0.33 – 0.41 0.41 ). Future work should explore vocabulary-controlled metrics or language pairs matched on tokenizer overlap.

All metrics are computed independently per layer ℓ \ell on the FLORES-200 devtest split.

sections.heading: GMM dominance per token ( λ \lambda ).
sections.text: Our metric builds on the GMM construction of Shani and Basirat (2025) . At each layer, embeddings H ℓ ∈ ℝ N × d H_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} are projected by PCA onto the smallest number of components n pca ​ ( ℓ ) n_{\text{pca}}(\ell) retaining ≥ 98 % \geq 98\% of the variance, with a floor of n pca ​ ( ℓ ) ≥ 2 n_{\text{pca}}(\ell)\geq 2 (matching the original implementation). A supervised Gaussian mixture is then fit with one full-covariance component per language; mean and covariance are estimated from per-language sample statistics rather than via expectation–maximization, and mixing weights are set proportional to per-language token counts: μ ^ k \displaystyle\hat{\mu}_{k} = 1 | S k | ​ ∑ i ∈ S k z ℓ ( i ) , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|S_{k}|}\sum_{i\in S_{k}}z_{\ell}^{(i)}, (1) Σ ^ k \displaystyle\hat{\Sigma}_{k} = 1 | S k | − 1 ​ ∑ i ∈ S k ( z ℓ ( i ) − μ ^ k ) ​ ( z ℓ ( i ) − μ ^ k ) ⊤ + ϵ ​ I , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{|S_{k}|-1}\sum_{i\in S_{k}}(z_{\ell}^{(i)}-\hat{\mu}_{k})(z_{\ell}^{(i)}-\hat{\mu}_{k})^{\top}+\epsilon I, (2) π ^ k \displaystyle\hat{\pi}_{k} = | S k | / N , \displaystyle=|S_{k}|/N, (3) where z ℓ ( i ) = PCA ℓ ​ ( h ℓ ( i ) ) z_{\ell}^{(i)}=\mathrm{PCA}_{\ell}(h_{\ell}^{(i)}) and S k = { i : ℓ ⁡ ( i ) = k } S_{k}=\{i:\ell(i)=k\} . The ridge ϵ = 10 − 4 \epsilon=10^{-4} is our addition, ensuring positive-definiteness for near-singular per-language covariances. Given the fitted mixture, every hidden state h h has a posterior P ⁡ ( ℓ ∣ h ) P(\ell\mid h) under each language Gaussian. For a token i i from source language s ⁡ ( i ) s(i) , we form the source-against-best-competitor ratio Λ ℓ ​ ( i ) = P ⁡ ( s ⁡ ( i ) ∣ h ℓ ( i ) ) max t ≠ s ⁡ ( i ) ⁡ P ⁡ ( t ∣ h ℓ ( i ) ) , \Lambda_{\ell}(i)\;=\;\frac{P\!\bigl(s(i)\mid h_{\ell}^{(i)}\bigr)}{\max_{t\neq s(i)}P\!\bigl(t\mid h_{\ell}^{(i)}\bigr)}, (4) which is a token-level instance of the pairwise likelihood ratio of Shani and Basirat (2025) (their Eq. 4), aggregated over foreign languages by retaining only the most competitive one. The layer-wise dominance fraction is the proportion of tokens for which this ratio falls below one, λ ⁡ ( ℓ ) = 1 N ​ | { i : Λ ℓ ​ ( i ) < 1 } | , \lambda(\ell)\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\,\bigl|\{i:\Lambda_{\ell}(i)<1\}\bigr|, (5) computed jointly across all source languages. The per-model summary reported in Table 1 is the peak-layer value λ ⋆ = max ℓ ⁡ λ ⁡ ( ℓ ) \lambda^{\star}=\max_{\ell}\lambda(\ell) .

sections.heading: Relation to the per-language dominance score.
sections.text: Our λ \lambda corresponds to the per-token analysis of Shani and Basirat (2025, §5.2) and is distinct from the per-language dominance score D ^ i ​ ( T ) = 𝔼 S ≠ T ​ 𝔼 h ∼ S ​ [ P ⁡ ( T ∣ h ) ] \hat{D}_{i}(T)=\mathbb{E}_{S\neq T}\,\mathbb{E}_{h\sim S}[P(T\mid h)] they develop in their §5.1 to test for a single mediating language. The dominance score is a scalar per target language. λ \lambda instead asks, for every token, whether the source-language Gaussian retains the largest posterior, and reports the population fraction for which it does not. The two metrics answer complementary questions and need not move together: D ^ i ​ ( T ) \hat{D}_{i}(T) tests whether one language acts as a representational magnet for the others, whereas λ \lambda measures the extent to which per-language regions of the embedding space remain linearly separable, irrespective of whether any single language dominates the rest. We compute three variants of λ \lambda that differ only in what counts as a token: • Word-level λ \lambda : tokens are kept at their natural per-language frequencies. • Sample-balanced λ \lambda (default reported in the main paper): each language is subsampled to 10,000 10{,}000 tokens before PCA fitting and GMM evaluation, matching the ILO subsampling protocol and removing tokenizer-fertility bias. • Sentence-level λ \lambda : h ℓ ( i ) h_{\ell}^{(i)} is replaced by the mean of token hidden states over sentence i i , giving one embedding per sentence. PCA hyperparameters are identical across the three variants.

sections.heading: Effective dimensionality and mean random cosine similarity.
sections.text: At each layer we report two anisotropy diagnostics computed on the same pooled hidden states used by λ \lambda : n pca ​ ( ℓ ) \displaystyle n_{\text{pca}}(\ell) = min ⁡ { k : ∑ j ≤ k σ j 2 ​ ( ℓ ) ∑ j σ j 2 ​ ( ℓ ) ≥ 0.98 } , \displaystyle=\min\Bigl\{k\,:\,\tfrac{\sum_{j\leq k}\sigma_{j}^{2}(\ell)}{\sum_{j}\sigma_{j}^{2}(\ell)}\geq 0.98\Bigr\}, (6) cos ¯ ​ ( ℓ ) \displaystyle\overline{\cos}(\ell) = 1 M ​ ∑ m = 1 M cos ⁡ ( h ℓ ( i m ) , h ℓ ( j m ) ) , \displaystyle=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\cos\bigl(h_{\ell}^{(i_{m})},\,h_{\ell}^{(j_{m})}\bigr), (7) where { σ j ​ ( ℓ ) } \{\sigma_{j}(\ell)\} are the singular values of the centered hidden-state matrix and { ( i m , j m ) } m = 1 M \{(i_{m},j_{m})\}_{m=1}^{M} are M = 5,000 M=5{,}000 pairs of distinct indices sampled uniformly at random with a fixed seed.

sections.heading: Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO).
sections.text: We follow the implementation of Wilie et al. (2025) . At layer ℓ \ell , all hidden states across languages are pooled into one matrix H ℓ H_{\ell} , and for every point i i we retrieve its k = 5 k=5 nearest neighbors under cosine similarity, 𝒩 k ​ ( i ) \mathcal{N}_{k}(i) , excluding self-similarity. Let L k ​ ( i ) = { ℓ ⁡ ( j ) : j ∈ 𝒩 k ​ ( i ) } ∖ { ℓ ⁡ ( i ) } L_{k}(i)=\{\ell(j):j\in\mathcal{N}_{k}(i)\}\setminus\{\ell(i)\} be the set of other languages appearing among i i ’s neighbors. The bridge score for language a a is Bridge a ( ℓ ) = | { i ∈ S a : | L k ​ ( i ) | ≥ τ } | | S a | , \mathrm{Bridge}_{a}(\ell)\;=\;\frac{|\{i\in S_{a}:|L_{k}(i)|\geq\tau\}|}{|S_{a}|}, (8) with threshold τ = 3 \tau=3 . The reachability score counts the distinct other languages appearing in any neighbor set of any point of a a and is normalized by L − 1 L-1 : Reach a ​ ( ℓ ) = 1 L − 1 ​ | ⋃ i ∈ S a L k ​ ( i ) | . \mathrm{Reach}_{a}(\ell)\;=\;\frac{1}{L-1}\,\Bigl|\bigcup_{i\in S_{a}}L_{k}(i)\Bigr|. (9) The per-language ILO score is the harmonic mean of the two, ILO a ​ ( ℓ ) = 2 ​ Bridge a ​ ( ℓ ) ​ Reach a ​ ( ℓ ) Bridge a ​ ( ℓ ) + Reach a ​ ( ℓ ) , \mathrm{ILO}_{a}(\ell)\;=\;\frac{2\,\mathrm{Bridge}_{a}(\ell)\,\mathrm{Reach}_{a}(\ell)}{\mathrm{Bridge}_{a}(\ell)+\mathrm{Reach}_{a}(\ell)}, (10) (set to 0 0 if either term is 0 0 ), and the layer score is the mean over languages, ILO ⁡ ( ℓ ) = L − 1 ​ ∑ a ILO a ​ ( ℓ ) \mathrm{ILO}(\ell)=L^{-1}\sum_{a}\mathrm{ILO}_{a}(\ell) . All ILO results in the paper use this word-level computation, subsampled to 10,000 10{,}000 tokens per language to equalize representation in the kNN graph (using a fixed seed); the sentence-level variant of the released implementation is reported in Appendix B.5 . We use k = 5 k=5 , τ = 3 \tau=3 , and cosine similarity throughout, matching the defaults of the released implementation of Wilie et al. (2025) (described there as the best settings).

sections.heading: Centered ILO ( ILO c \mathrm{ILO}_{c} ).
sections.text: We define ILO c \mathrm{ILO}_{c} identically to ILO \mathrm{ILO} but on mean-subtracted hidden states. Concretely, at each layer ℓ \ell we compute the sample-weighted grand mean over the pooled (post-subsampling) embeddings, h ¯ ℓ = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N h ℓ ( i ) , \bar{h}_{\ell}\;=\;\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}h_{\ell}^{(i)}, (11) and replace every h ℓ ( i ) h_{\ell}^{(i)} with h ℓ ( i ) − h ¯ ℓ h_{\ell}^{(i)}-\bar{h}_{\ell} before running kNN. Subtracting the same vector from every language preserves cross-lingual offsets but removes the shared anisotropic “common direction” ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ) .

sections.heading: Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA).
sections.text: For a language pair ( a , b ) (a,b) and layer ℓ \ell , let X ∈ ℝ n × d X\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} and Y ∈ ℝ n × d Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} be the matrices of mean-pooled sentence embeddings for the n n FLORES sentence pairs. Linear CKA ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) is CKA ⁡ ( X , Y ) = ‖ Y ⊤ ​ X ‖ F 2 ‖ X ⊤ ​ X ‖ F ​ ‖ Y ⊤ ​ Y ‖ F , \mathrm{CKA}(X,Y)\;=\;\frac{\|Y^{\top}X\|_{F}^{2}}{\|X^{\top}X\|_{F}\,\|Y^{\top}Y\|_{F}}, (12) computed after centering each column of X X and Y Y . We aggregate over the ( L 2 ) \binom{L}{2} language pairs and over layers by simple averaging; the per-model summary in Table 1 is the layer-mean of the language-pair mean.

sections.heading: Average Neuron Correlation (ANC).
sections.text: For the same X , Y X,Y , ANC ( Del and Fishel, 2022 ) measures alignment at the level of individual neurons: ANC ( X , Y ) = 1 d ∑ j = 1 d | ρ ( X : , j , Y : , j ) | , \mathrm{ANC}(X,Y)\;=\;\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^{d}\bigl|\rho\bigl(X_{:,j},Y_{:,j}\bigr)\bigr|, (13) where ρ \rho is the Pearson correlation across the n n aligned sentence pairs and the absolute value accounts for sign-flips that are immaterial to neuron function. We aggregate over language pairs and layers as for CKA.

sections.heading: A.3 Computational Cost
sections.text: We state asymptotic per-layer costs in the notation of § A.2 ( d d : hidden size; n = 1,012 n=1{,}012 parallel sentences for the sentence-level metrics; N = 10 5 N=10^{5} pooled tokens for the token-level metrics). ANC computes d d Pearson correlations over n n aligned samples per language pair: O ⁡ ( n ​ d ) O(nd) time. CKA additionally requires a matrix product: O ⁡ ( n ​ d ⋅ min ⁡ ( n , d ) ) O(nd\cdot\min(n,d)) per pair. λ \lambda is dominated by the PCA of the N × d N\times d matrix of pooled hidden states: O ⁡ ( N ​ d 2 ) O(Nd^{2}) for N > d N>d . ILO retrieves exact nearest neighbors over all N N pooled points, an all-pairs computation of O ⁡ ( N 2 ​ d ) O(N^{2}d) ; since N N is two orders of magnitude larger than n n , ILO is the most expensive of the four. Memory is dominated by the pooled hidden states, O ⁡ ( N ​ d ) O(Nd) , about 2 2 GB per layer at single precision for N = 10 5 N=10^{5} and d = 5,120 d=5{,}120 .

sections.heading: A.4 Language Probe Setup
sections.text: The language probe is a multinomial logistic regression over L = 10 L=10 FLORES languages, trained per layer in three feature spaces: • Full : the raw hidden state h ℓ ∈ ℝ d h_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} . • PCA principal : projection onto the top n pca ​ ( ℓ ) n_{\text{pca}}(\ell) PCA components retaining ≥ 98 % \geq 98\% of variance (the same components λ \lambda operates on, with the same floor of 2 2 ). • PCA residual : projection onto the orthogonal complement, the remaining d − n pca ​ ( ℓ ) d-n_{\text{pca}}(\ell) components.

sections.heading: Hyperparameters.
sections.text: We use a stratified 80/20 split over the L × 1,012 L\times 1{,}012 FLORES-200 sentences. The classifier is multinomial logistic regression with L 2 L_{2} regularization, trained by L-BFGS with strong Wolfe line search, tol_grad = 10 − 5 \text{tol\_grad}=10^{-5} , tol_change = 10 − 9 \text{tol\_change}=10^{-9} , and at most 1,000 1{,}000 iterations. Features are not standardized; using raw PCA scores keeps the three subspaces directly comparable in scale (the PCA principal subspace already contains the high-variance directions). We report test-set accuracy.

sections.heading: A.5 Cross-lingual Finetuning Datasets
sections.text: We use five established benchmarks for the transfer evaluation (§ 4.3 ); per-language coverage and split sizes are given in Table 5 . • Belebele ( Bandarkar et al., 2024 ) : multiple-choice reading comprehension, 4-way. We train on the belebele_training_set (English, ≈ \approx 71 K examples) and evaluate on the test set in 10 languages. • XNLI ( Conneau et al., 2018 ) : 3-way natural language inference, parallel across 15 languages. We train on the English train split ( ≈ \approx 392 K examples) and evaluate on the test split for the 8 of our 10 languages present in XNLI (Japanese and Portuguese excluded). • XCSR ( Lin et al., 2021 ) : 5-way multilingual commonsense reasoning. We train on the English X-CSQA train split ( ≈ \approx 9.7 K examples) and evaluate on the validation split for the 9 covered target languages. • SIB-200 ( Adelani et al., 2024 ) : 7-way topic classification on FLORES-200 sentences. We train on the per-language train split (701 examples) and evaluate on the test split in all 10 languages. • XQuAD ( Artetxe et al., 2020 ) : extractive QA. Following standard practice, we train on the English SQuAD v1.1 train split ( ≈ \approx 87.6 K examples) and evaluate F1 on the XQuAD test sets for the 7 covered target languages. The transfer score for each model is the unweighted mean of the five per-task means, each computed over that task’s non-English target languages. sections.heading: Optimizer and schedule.
sections.text: For every (model, task) pair we finetune with AdamW (PyTorch defaults β 1 = 0.9 \beta_{1}=0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 \beta_{2}=0.999 , ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} ), weight decay 0.01 0.01 , gradient clipping at ℓ 2 \ell_{2} norm 1.0 1.0 , linear warmup over the first 10 % 10\% of training steps followed by linear decay to zero, and maximum sequence length 512 512 . Models are trained in bfloat16 mixed precision on A100/H200 GPUs. The classification head is a fresh task-specific linear layer on top of the last-layer hidden state of the final non-padding token; QA training uses standard span prediction heads. All other model parameters are unfrozen.

sections.heading: Per-task budget.
sections.text: Effective batch size and epoch count per task are: XNLI, XCSR, XQuAD (eff. batch 32 32 , 3 epochs for the larger tasks; 20 epochs for XCSR); SIB-200 (eff. batch 32 32 , 20 epochs); Belebele (eff. batch 16 16 , 3 epochs). For tasks with a validation split (XNLI, XCSR, SIB-200) we select the epoch with the lowest validation cross-entropy and use that checkpoint for downstream evaluation; for tasks without a validation split (Belebele, XQuAD) we use the final-epoch model.

sections.text: For each (model, task) pair we sweep over 3–5 learning rates drawn from { × 10 − 6 , × 10 − 6 , 10 − 5 , × 10 − 5 , × 10 − 5 , 10 − 4 , × 10 − 4 , × 10 − 4 , 10 − 3 , × 10 − 3 } \{2\!\times\!10^{-6},\,5\!\times\!10^{-6},\,10^{-5},\,2\!\times\!10^{-5},\,5\!\times\!10^{-5},\,10^{-4},\,2\!\times\!10^{-4},\,5\!\times\!10^{-4},\,10^{-3},\,2\!\times\!10^{-3}\} , with the range adapted to each family’s stable regime (BLOOM, OPT and Qwen3 stable at 10 − 5 10^{-5} – 10 − 4 10^{-4} ; XGLM stable at × 10 − 5 5\!\times\!10^{-5} – 10 − 3 10^{-3} ). When the best LR sat at a sweep boundary we extended the range until either an interior optimum was found or the boundary remained stable.

sections.heading: Granularity of λ \lambda .
sections.text: Figures 26 – 30 compare three computations of λ \lambda within each family: sample-balanced (10,000 tokens per language; used elsewhere in the paper), word-level (all token positions on the same GMM), and sentence-level (mean-pooled sentence embeddings). Sample-balanced and word-level λ \lambda track each other closely across all 21 models, validating the sampling choice used in the main analysis. Sentence-level λ \lambda diverges along family lines: it is zero throughout all layers for BLOOM, OPT, and XGLM, indicating that sentence-mean pooling collapses the cluster structure that token-level inputs preserve. In Qwen3 and SmolLM3 it instead shows a sharp early-layer peak (relative depth ≤ 0.37 \leq 0.37 ) reaching 0.41 0.41 – 0.56 0.56 , well below the sample-balanced and word-level peaks ( ≈ 0.85 \approx 0.85 – 0.91 0.91 ) but clearly non-zero; the peak narrows as Qwen3 scales from 0.6B to 14B. These granularities also address whether the metrics’ different input units explain the cross-metric disagreement of § 4.2 : the disagreements occur within each input class, since CKA and ANC are computed from identical sentence embeddings yet correlate with transfer at ρ = 0.14 \rho=0.14 and 0.84 0.84 , while λ \lambda and ILO are computed from identical token samples yet give opposite verdicts on XGLM ( λ = 0.03 \lambda=0.03 , ILO = 0.44 =0.44 ). If the input unit were the cause, metrics sharing a unit would agree; instead, the metrics that fail are those exposed to the common-shift geometry (CKA) or confined to the collapsed principal subspace ( λ \lambda ), irrespective of unit. These methods have been developed largely in isolation, and when they disagree, it is unclear whether the disagreement reflects a property of the model or an artifact of the measurement. We compare four sharing metrics —CKA, ANC, GMM dominance per token, and ILO —across 21 base models from five families (125M–14B parameters) and correlate each with cross-lingual transfer on five downstream tasks. We find that the metrics differ in their quantification of cross-lingual sharing in these models and suggest that the disagreement traces to anisotropy , the tendency of representations to cluster in a narrow cone of the embedding space. Only ILO’s correlation with cross-lingual transfer (Spearman’s ρ = 0.90 \rho=0.90 ) survives controls for model size, family, and per-task variation. We therefore recommend ILO as the primary sharing metric, to be reported alongside anisotropy diagnostics. Figure 1: Sentence embeddings at layer 18 of Qwen3-8B-Base, projected to 2D via PCA. Left: Embeddings exhibit anisotropy in that they form a narrow cone offset from the origin. Right: Removing the top-2 principal components yields a significantly more isotropic residual. We show that language identity is largely relocated to this residual (§ 4.2 ), implying that sharing metrics that explicitly or implicitly focus on the principal subspace will be unreliable. 1 Introduction Multilingual language models develop shared representations across languages without explicit alignment supervision ( Pires et al., 2019 ; Wu and Dredze, 2019 ) . A growing set of interpretability methods now claims to measure this sharing: probing classifiers, similarity metrics, distributional approaches, and neuron-level analyses. These methods have largely been developed in isolation, on one or two model families at a time. When different metrics on different models yield different conclusions, it is unclear whether the disagreement reflects genuine differences between models or is an artifact of the measurement itself. This ambiguity is especially concerning as contextual embeddings often exhibit anisotropy : they occupy a narrow cone in the representation space, rather than spreading evenly in all directions ( isotropy ), with variance concentrated in a few dimensions ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ; Timkey and van Schijndel, 2021 ) , as shown in Figure 1 . Anisotropy poses at least two risks for any geometric measure of cross-lingual sharing: First, it inflates apparent similarity, making any two vectors look close by default. Second, it confines meaningful variation to a low-dimensional subspace, so any metric sensitive to dominant directions of variance —whether it explicitly projects onto them or implicitly up-weights them —will be driven by that subspace rather than by the full representational geometry. Because conclusions about which architectures, training regimes, and scaling choices yield stronger cross-lingual sharing are only as reliable as the metrics on which they rest, it matters whether metrics can be trusted to track sharing through anisotropy. This paper therefore examines how this distortion affects the metrics under consideration, and assesses which, if any, can be relied on to reflect genuine cross-lingual sharing. Concretely, we address three questions through a systematic comparison of four sharing metrics across 21 base models from five families (BLOOM, OPT, XGLM, Qwen3, SmolLM3; 125M–14B parameters), supplemented by instruction-tuned variants and intermediate checkpoints: • How do multilingual models share representations across languages? • When do existing metrics agree or disagree as to the degree of cross-lingual sharing? • Which metric best predicts cross-lingual transfer? Our answers, anticipating § 4 : models exhibit three sharing patterns rather than a binary split implied by metrics dominated by high-variance directions, and the metric disagreement traces directly to anisotropy, with language probes showing that language identity is relocated to the directions such metrics discard or down-weight. Among the four metrics, ILO ( Wilie et al., 2025 ) is the only one whose association with cross-lingual transfer survives controls for size, family, and per-task variation, reaching a Spearman rank correlation of ρ = 0.90 \rho=0.90 ; ANC ( Del and Fishel, 2022 ) forms a clear second tier whose association rests on between-family contrasts, while PCA-based GMM dominance per token ( Shani and Basirat, 2025 ) has a within-family signal too weak to characterize as a relationship across matched architectures and CKA ( Kornblith et al., 2019 ) shows no association at any level. We therefore recommend ILO as the primary sharing metric, and further suggest that it should be reported alongside anisotropy diagnostics. 2 Related Work Measuring cross-lingual sharing Multilingual models develop shared representations between languages without explicit alignment supervision ( Pires et al., 2019 ; Wu and Dredze, 2019 ) . The contributing factors remain debated; shared positional embeddings, similar word order, parameter sharing across languages, and training-data imbalance have all been proposed as drivers ( Dufter and Schütze, 2020 ; Conneau et al., 2020b ; Schäfer et al., 2024 ) . A series of measures has been developed to quantify cross-lingual sharing: Similarity-based metrics compare activation patterns across languages on parallel input. Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA; Kornblith et al., 2019 ) measures global geometric similarity between cross-lingual representation matrices. Average Neuron Correlation (ANC; Del and Fishel, 2022 ) captures per-neuron alignment. Lens-based methods such as the logit lens ( nostalgebraist, 2020 ) project intermediate hidden states into the vocabulary. Wendler et al. (2024) use this to argue that Llama-2 routes multilingual inputs through English-aligned representations. Subsequent work has questioned both the technique ( Belrose et al., 2025 ) and the claim itself: apparent reliance on English varies with training data balance, and representations often mix from several languages rather than being pivoted toward English ( Zhong et al., 2025 ; Schut et al., 2025 ; Trinley et al., 2025 ; Harrasse et al., 2026 ) . Shani and Basirat (2025) present a mixture model-based metric : they fit Gaussian mixture models over PCA-projected representations and use them to derive language dominance scores. Wilie et al. (2025) introduce Interlingual Local Overlap (ILO), a neighborhood-based metric that operates on the full hidden state. Finally, neuron-level analyses identify units that activate selectively per language, using activation entropy ( Tang et al., 2024 ; Kojima et al., 2024 ) , ternary classifications ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , sparse autoencoders ( Deng et al., 2025 ) , or transcoders ( Harrasse et al., 2026 ) . A parallel line of work scores each language by its directed alignment with English and validates it against downstream performance, at the language level in MEXA ( Kargaran et al., 2025 ) and at the instance level in DALI ( Ravisankar et al., 2026 ) . These primarily measure alignment with English rather than sharing among all languages, which is what the four metrics we compare quantify; we relate the two views in Appendix C.4 . All of these methods have largely been developed and evaluated in isolation. Comparisons typically restrict themselves to one or two model families, leaving open whether disagreements between metrics reflect substantive differences between models or measurement artifacts. Filling this gap, we compare four representative metrics —spanning similarity-based, distributional, and neighborhood approaches —on the same set of models (§ 4 ). Representational anisotropy Contextual embeddings from transformer models tend to occupy a narrow cone in representation space rather than filling it isotropically, with most pairs of vectors having high cosine similarity regardless of their semantic content ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ; Gao et al., 2019 ) . Biś et al. (2021) argue that much of this apparent anisotropy stems from a common shift shared across embeddings: once the mean is subtracted, the residual distribution is closer to isotropic. Other proposed causes of anisotropy include self-attention dynamics ( Godey et al., 2024 ) and optimizer-level effects in Adam ( Stollenwerk and Stollenwerk, 2025 ) . Regardless of cause, anisotropy distorts geometric analyses of representations. Rajaee and Pilehvar (2022) and Hämmerl et al. (2023) document anisotropy in multilingual models specifically, and show that post-hoc isotropy enhancement improves cross-lingual semantic similarity —indicating that anisotropy can mask genuine cross-lingual structure. How isotropy should be measured is itself contested ( Rudman et al., 2022 ) , and anisotropy is not uniformly harmful: it has limited impact on sentence-representation expressiveness for clustering ( Ait-Saada and Nadif, 2023 ) , is incompatible with cluster structure by construction ( Mickus et al., 2024 ) , and decreasing isotropy during finetuning can improve downstream performance ( Rudman and Eickhoff, 2024 ) . Our concern is not whether anisotropy is desirable in a model, but what it does to the metrics used to measure cross-lingual sharing (§ 4.2 ); our own diagnosis there rests on effective dimensionality and probing rather than on the cosine diagnostic alone. 3 Experimental Setup In our main experiments, we compute four cross-lingual sharing metrics across 21 models. This section presents these metrics and models along with the data we used and our statistical framework. 3.1 Sharing Metrics We select one metric from each of the main methodological families of representation-level cross-lingual analysis, so that the comparison contrasts kinds of measurement rather than variants of one kind: CKA for global geometric similarity, ANC for neuron-level correspondence, λ \lambda for distributional structure, and ILO for local neighborhood overlap. The metrics are: • (Linear) CKA (Centered Kernel Alignment; Kornblith et al., 2019 ) is the established geometric-similarity baseline. It measures the similarity between two representation spaces by comparing their pairwise distance structures —specifically, how consistently pairs of representations that are similar in one space are also similar in the other. Values range from 0 (no shared structure) to 1 (identical up to isotropic scaling and orthogonal transformation). • ANC (Average Neuron-Wise Correlation; Del and Fishel, 2022 ) measures whether individual neurons carry consistent activation patterns across languages —in contrast to CKA, which measures whether the overall pairwise similarity structure is preserved across representations. For each neuron, ANC computes the absolute Pearson correlation between its activations on parallel sentences in two languages. Averaging over neurons yields a value in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] , where 1 indicates that every neuron responds identically (up to sign differences) across languages. • GMM dominance per token. Shani and Basirat (2025) fit a supervised Gaussian Mixture Model in a PCA subspace retaining 98% of variance and report the fraction of tokens whose likelihood is higher in a foreign-language space than in their own. We refer to this quantity as λ \lambda and report it by layer after subsampling each language to 10,000 tokens before PCA and GMM fitting. This matches the subsampling used for ILO and removes tokenizer-fertility bias as a confound when comparing across families with different scripts. Unbalanced word-level and sentence-level variants appear in Appendix A.2 . • ILO (Interlingual Local Overlap; Wilie et al., 2025 ) quantifies cross-lingual sharing via k k -nearest-neighbor queries ( k = 5 k=5 ) in the full representation space, combining bridge scores (how often a token’s neighbors include other languages) and reachability scores (the fraction of other languages that appear in the k k -nearest-neighbor set of any token of that language) into a single index ranging from 0 (complete separation) to 1 (complete sharing). We compute ILO on token-level representations with the same 10,000-tokens-per-language subsample as λ \lambda , which controls tokenizer fertility. The released implementation of Wilie et al. (2025) instead operates on mean-pooled sentence embeddings; we report that variant in Appendix B.5 . We additionally report a centered variant (ILO c ), computed identically after subtracting the per-layer mean hidden state across all tokens and languages, which removes anisotropy-driven neighborhood structure that can inflate apparent sharing. 3.2 Models Our 21 base models come from five model families, spanning 125M to 14B parameters and varying in training data composition and scale. We briefly introduce the model families here; see Appendix A.1 for full details on models and checkpoints. • BLOOM BigScience Workshop et al. (2023) (560M–7.1B) is trained on 350B tokens of the ROOTS corpus Laurençon et al. (2022) . It covers 46 natural languages with ca. 70% non-English data, and provides pretraining checkpoints. • XGLM Lin et al. (2022) (564M–7.5B) is trained on 30 languages drawn from CC100-XL. We use both BLOOM and XGLM despite their age because the sharing metrics we evaluate were validated on these families: Shani and Basirat (2025) report λ \lambda on BLOOM and Del and Fishel (2022) report ANC on XGLM. • OPT Zhang et al. (2022) (125M–6.7B) serves as our non-multilingual baseline. It is trained on 180B predominantly English tokens from the Pile Gao et al. (2020) , BookCorpus, and CC-News, with only incidental non-English content from Common Crawl. • Qwen3 Yang et al. (2025) (0.6B–14B) provides a modern high-compute comparison. It is trained on ca. 36T tokens spanning 119 languages and dialects, though exact proportions are undisclosed. • SmolLM3 Bakouch et al. (2025) (3B) is trained on 11.2T tokens drawn primarily from FineWeb-Edu, FineWeb-2, and DCLM, with ca. 12% multilingual web data natively supporting six languages (English, French, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese) plus additional training on Arabic, Chinese, and Russian; it uniquely provides intermediate checkpoints across three training stages for studying multilingual representations during pre- and post-training. We additionally characterize instruction-tuned variants —BLOOMZ Muennighoff et al. (2023) , Qwen3 non-Base, SmolLM3-Instruct —and 59 intermediate checkpoints from BLOOM and SmolLM3, yielding a total of 32 model configurations plus checkpoints. Instruction-tuned variants contribute to representational characterization but are excluded from transfer analysis; all transfer correlations are based on the 21 base models. This is because our transfer protocol finetunes on English data and evaluates zero-shot (§ 3.4 ), measuring what the pretraining geometry makes possible; on instruction-tuned variants it would entangle sharing with post-training recipes that differ across families. The question we do ask about post-training—whether it changes the sharing structure—is addressed in § 4.4 . 3.3 Data All interpretability analyses use the FLORES-200 NLLB Team et al. (2022) devtest set, providing 1,012 parallel sentences across ten languages: Arabic, Chinese, English, French, German, Japanese, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, and Turkish. These languages span four scripts (Latin, Cyrillic, Arabic, CJK), multiple typological families (Romance, Germanic, Turkic, Japonic, Sino-Tibetan, Semitic, Slavic), and a range of morphological types (isolating, fusional, agglutinative). Sentence-level pairs are required by CKA and ANC, which compute cross-lingual similarity from aligned representations; the remaining methods operate on monolingual representations. 3.4 Cross-Lingual Transfer Evaluation We use zero-shot cross-lingual transfer as a functional validation criterion, not as ground truth for sharing: transfer has drivers beyond representational alignment, among them task format, vocabulary overlap, and target-language pretraining exposure, which is why we average over five tasks, require associations to survive a number of controls (§ 3.5 ), and keep the diagnosis of the disagreement between methods (§ 4.2 ) independent of transfer. We fine-tune each of the 21 base models on English training data and evaluate zero-shot on up to nine non-English languages (coverage varies by task; Appendix A.5 ) across five tasks: Belebele (reading comprehension; Bandarkar et al., 2024 ), XNLI (natural language inference; Conneau et al., 2018 ), XCSR (commonsense reasoning; Lin et al., 2021 ), SIB-200 (topic classification; Adelani et al., 2024 ), and XQuAD (extractive question answering; Artetxe et al., 2020 ). As an aggregate per-model metric, we compute, for each task, the mean accuracy over the non-English target languages that task covers, and then take the unweighted mean of these five per-task means. We refer to this number as the transfer score . For each model–task pair, we sweep over 3–5 learning rates between 5 × 10 − 6 5\times 10^{-6} and 10 − 4 10^{-4} , with ranges adapted to the model family’s stable regime. We use AdamW with linear warmup (10% of steps), weight decay 0.01, and gradient clipping at 1.0. Task-specific epoch counts range from 3 to 20. The best learning rate is selected for each model–task pair based on validation accuracy. Full hyperparameters are in Appendix A.6 . Because the § 4.3 correlations link base model metrics to finetuned model behavior, we re-apply the full interpretability suite after finetuning to verify that the base model geometry survives. 3.5 Statistical Framework Beyond characterizing representations, we test for functional relevance: whether sharing metrics correlate with cross-lingual transfer, and whether any association survives controls for model size, family membership, and task choice. Primary correlation We use Spearman rank correlations ( ρ \rho ) for all tests. The primary correlation is computed across all models relative to the transfer score defined in § 3.4 . Decompositions We report three additional analyses to check whether the primary correlation is robust. Per-family ρ \rho separates between- from within-family contributions to the cross-model association. Per-task ρ \rho for each metric against each task (4 metrics × \times 5 tasks = = 20 tests) shows whether the primary correlation holds task by task. Because running 20 tests simultaneously inflates the family-wise false-positive rate, we apply the Benjamini and Hochberg (1995) procedure, which bounds the expected proportion of false discoveries among reported associations at α = 0.05 \alpha=0.05 . This ensures that a pattern such as a correlation being significant across all five tasks reflects a consistent relationship rather than accumulated chance. Partial Spearman ρ \rho controlling for log 10 \log_{10} parameter size checks that the sharing–transfer association is not reducible to a model-size effect. Within most families, parameter count correlates with both cross-lingual sharing and transfer performance, raising the possibility that any observed association between sharing and transfer is a spurious consequence of larger models doing everything better rather than a genuine relationship between the two. Partialling out log 10 \log_{10} parameters removes the variance in both sharing and transfer that is attributable to size, so that the residual correlation reflects whether sharing predicts transfer over and above what model size alone would explain. Permutation tests Given our small sample size, we verify significance with non-parametric permutation tests. Each test recomputes ρ \rho on 10,000 random shuffles of the transfer score values to estimate the null distribution, from which we compute a one-tailed p p -value as the proportion of recomputed ρ \rho values greater than or equal to the observed ρ \rho . We run two designs: The first shuffles across all models, testing whether any monotonic association exists. The second shuffles within each family only, testing whether the association persists once between-family contrasts are removed. Family membership is otherwise a confound: model families differ systematically in both architecture and training data, so the cross-model correlation could be driven entirely by between-family contrasts. 3.6 Additional Diagnostics In addition to the sharing metrics, we report two diagnostics at each layer. Effective dimensionality ( n pca n_{\text{pca}} ) is the number of PCA components needed to retain 98% of variance; small values relative to the full number of dimensions indicate that representations occupy a low-dimensional subspace. Mean random cosine similarity is the average cosine between 5,000 random pairs of hidden states; high values indicate the “narrow cone” geometry where any two vectors look similar by default ( Ethayarajh, 2019 ) , biasing similarity-based measures upward. Together, these metrics flag layers where sharing metrics should be interpreted with caution. 4 Results and Discussion This section presents our main results together with additional analyses, and discusses our findings. We organize the section around four questions: 4.1 How Do Models Share Representations Across Languages? When we apply the four metrics across our 21 base models, three distinct sharing patterns emerge (cf. Table 1 , Figure 2 ). • Pattern 1: Concentrated sharing (BLOOM ≥ {\geq} 1B, Qwen3, SmolLM3): high λ \lambda ( > 0.75 >0.75 ), high ILO, and variance concentrated in just n pca = 2 n_{\text{pca}}=2 dimensions at the peak λ \lambda layer. The sharing metrics increase through the middle layers and fall toward the output, producing the inverted-U profile visible in Figure 2 . • Pattern 2: Distributed sharing (XGLM): high ILO ( 0.44 0.44 at 4.5B, comparable to BLOOM-7.1B’s 0.40 0.40 ) but near-zero λ \lambda , with variance distributed across thousands of dimensions ( n pca n_{\text{pca}} in the thousands at every layer). • Pattern 3: Minimal sharing (OPT): low values on every metric, consistent with OPT’s predominantly English training data. The critical case is XGLM. GMM dominance per token used in isolation groups XGLM with OPT, despite XGLM’s transfer score ( 0.55 0.55 ) approaching BLOOM-7.1B ( 0.60 0.60 ) and clearly exceeding OPT-6.7B ( 0.41 0.41 ). The remaining metrics tell a coherent story: across all 21 models, ANC spans 0.34 0.34 – 0.68 0.68 and tracks the sharing patterns, while CKA falls in a narrow band ( 0.58 0.58 – 0.73 0.73 ) and discriminates poorly across families.
